common_name: Will Goodwin Clematis (Large Pale Lavender-Blue Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Will Goodwin is an early large-flowered cultivar that blooms on both old and new wood, so needs only light pruning.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a trellis, arbor, or fence. Will Goodwin bears large, pale lavender-blue flowers with a soft, luminous quality and gently ruffled petal edges, opening earlier in the season than many large-flowered clematis and often reblooming lightly later in summer. Its clear, gentle color pairs well with roses and other early-summer perennials trained on the same support. Because it blooms on both old wood from the previous season and new growth, it needs only light, selective pruning in late winter to remove dead or weak stems rather than the hard annual cutback required by later-blooming, new-wood cultivars.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Crystal Fountain produces an unusual double, flower-within-a-flower form on old wood in early summer, with simpler single flowers reblooming later on new growth.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a trellis or obelisk. Crystal Fountain produces striking double flowers in early summer, with an outer ring of pale lavender-blue petals surrounding an inner tuft of shorter, similarly colored petaloid stamens that create a distinctive flower-within-a-flower effect, then reblooms later in summer with simpler, single flowers of the same soft color on new growth. This two-stage flowering means light pruning in late winter to remove only dead or damaged stems preserves the early double display, while the plant still produces a second flush later in the season regardless. Its unusual bloom form makes it a conversation piece trained on an arbor, obelisk, or fence.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Piilu is a compact, Estonian-bred clematis well suited to containers and small trellises, blooming on old wood with a second flush on new growth.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade, on a compact trellis, obelisk, or large container support. Piilu bears semi-double flowers in soft pink with a deeper pink central bar down each petal, opening earlier in the season on the previous year's growth and reblooming with simpler single flowers on new growth later in summer. Its shorter, more restrained vine habit than many large-flowered clematis makes it well suited to container growing, small trellises, or the front of a mixed border where a full-sized clematis would be too vigorous. Prune lightly in late winter, removing only dead or weak stems, to preserve the early double flush while still allowing continued bloom through the season.

common_name: Star of India Clematis (Classic Purple-Red with Red Bar)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Star of India is a long-cultivated Victorian-era cultivar that blooms on both old and new wood over a long summer season.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence. Star of India, introduced in the 1860s, bears large, rich purple-red flowers marked with a deeper carmine-red bar down the center of each petal, a bold, saturated color combination that has kept this Victorian-era cultivar in cultivation for well over a century. It blooms over a long season from early summer into fall on both old and new growth, and prune lightly in late winter, removing only dead or weak stems, to preserve the earliest flush while allowing the vine to keep flowering through summer.

common_name: Gipsy Queen Clematis (Deep Velvety Purple Viticella-Type)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Gipsy Queen blooms on new growth, so it can be cut back hard each late winter, an easier pruning regime than early-flowering cultivars require.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a trellis, arbor, or fence. Gipsy Queen bears richly saturated, velvety deep purple flowers with a subtle reddish sheen, blooming freely from midsummer into fall entirely on the current season's growth, which makes it one of the easiest clematis types to prune, since the entire vine can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter without sacrificing any of the coming season's bloom. Its vigorous, free-flowering habit and deep, dramatic color make it a strong choice for covering a fence or arbor quickly each year. This forgiving pruning regime also makes it a good choice for gardeners new to growing clematis.
